name: Zoe Zhang

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Zoe. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't linked to any company, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, and your name won't be attached to anything. Could you start by walking me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure. I lead the night shift at Kestrel Plastics, which is an injection moulding plant on the edge of town, by the river. We've got fourteen presses that squirt hot plastic into steel moulds and spit out car parts: door handle trims, vent grilles, little clips nobody ever notices. I come in at ten, walk the line with the day lead, check which moulds are running, then spend the night chasing short shots and flash and keeping six operators from falling asleep at four in the morning.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that I can hear when a press is wrong before the screen tells me, and the younger ones come to me for that. I like my crew, especially Bernie, who's been setting moulds for thirty years and still brings me soup in a flask. What wears me out is the pay, honestly. I'm one of the best on the floor and I still check my bank app before I buy groceries, and there's only one other moulding plant within an hour's drive.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Do you use any AI tools, at work or at home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: No. My partner Dani laughs at me for it. I don't trust them, and nobody's ever shown me one that would help me fix a sticking ejector pin at three in the morning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly hype. Okay, that one I can picture, because that's how most new things at Kestrel turn out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, probably in the break room with my feet up. The bosses brought in a fancy scheduling system two years ago and we still fix the plan on a whiteboard. I'd say the same thing at the union meeting: the hype was a way to scare us into accepting less.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be relieved, but it doesn't fix my real problem. My real problem is that I earn less than operators at the plant in Ridgeford and I've got about three weeks of rent in the bank. AI not happening doesn't give me a raise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I do. I'd push harder in the next pay talks, because if management can't blame robots then they've got no excuse. And I'd keep putting forty a month into the savings jar, which mostly gets raided when the car needs tyres.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A bit flat, because the normal I'm going back to isn't great either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said management would have no excuse. What excuse do they use now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right now it's always the car makers. The customer wants the price down three percent, so we get no raise. Last year they said it was energy prices. If it's not robots it'll be something, but at least then it's an old argument I know how to fight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Dani say if you came home and told her nothing's changing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd say good, now can we talk about you asking for days. She hates that we only see each other at weekends. That's the conversation we keep putting off, and AI going quiet wouldn't stop it.

S0.say: I told you so. The hype was a way to scare workers into accepting less, and now management has no excuse in pay talks.
S0.think: I'm relieved, but it doesn't fix my real problem. I earn less than operators in the next town and have about three weeks of rent saved.
S0.do: Keeps running the night shift as before and pushes harder in the next pay round through the union. Keeps putting about 40 a month aside, knowing it often goes on car repairs.
S0.feel: Calm and a little flat, because the normal she goes back to is still tight.
S0.quote: AI not happening doesn't give me a raise.
S0.fieldNote: Zoe treats AI hype as one more line management uses to hold down pay, like energy prices before it. Even in the calmest picture her focus is money and the night shift, not technology. The tension with Dani about working days came up unprompted and seems to weigh on her more than AI does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Many tasks in many jobs. Hm. In a moulding plant the obvious task is pulling parts out and packing them, and that's half my crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need a proper agreement before any of it comes in. No robot arm goes on a press without the union seeing the plan, and anyone moved off a press gets trained and kept on at the same pay. I'd say it loud at the meeting and I'd say it to the plant manager's face.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think it means the floor shrinks around me. They'll keep a few people like me who can troubleshoot, maybe, but they already put a picker arm on press six last spring and that job is gone. Kelly used to run six. She works at the supermarket now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get the union to ask for the automation plan in writing in the first month. I'd cut what I can, which isn't much: no takeaway, cancel the streaming. And I'd write to our local representative, because there should be a law that a company has to retrain people before it replaces them. I wouldn't go on some online course, though. I'm not paying out of my own pocket to train my own replacement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tight in the chest. Like when a mould starts flashing and you know the whole run is going to be scrap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you wouldn't train your own replacement. If the company offered to pay for a robot technician course, would you take it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not, if I'm honest. I know what I'm good at and it's the press, the smell of it, the sound of it. Dani would kill me for saying that, because it's the sensible thing. Maybe if Bernie did it with me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on your crew would you worry about first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Marta, on the packing table. She's forty-something, her English isn't great, and she's quicker than any machine I've seen, but nobody hires for quick hands anymore. I'd want the union to fight for her before me.

S1.say: No robot arm goes on a press until the union has seen the plan, and anyone moved off a press must be retrained and kept on at the same pay.
S1.think: The floor shrinks around me and maybe a few troubleshooters like me survive. The picker arm on press six already cost Kelly her job.
S1.do: Gets the union to demand the automation plan in writing in the first month and cuts takeaways and streaming. Writes to her local representative asking for a law that makes firms retrain people before replacing them, but refuses to pay for courses herself.
S1.feel: A tight chest, like watching a run turn to scrap and knowing you can't stop it.
S1.quote: I'm not paying out of my own pocket to train my own replacement.
S1.fieldNote: Zoe's resistance to change and her politics point the same way: she would rather fight for the job than prepare to leave it. She admitted that refusing a paid course isn't sensible, then defended it as loyalty to the press. Her first concern was for Marta on the packing table rather than herself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. By 2028. That's before my car loan's even paid off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a choice that rich people are making, not weather. I'd be out with the union, I'd be posting about it, I'd be saying the government has to step in with income support and stop firms from dumping whole shifts overnight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly? I think I'm finished in that plant. If a robot can fix a stuck ejector pin and swap a mould, then the night lead is the first cost they cut, because nights cost more. And there's nowhere else around here to go. Ridgeford would be doing the same thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First week, I'd sit down with Dani and the bank app and work out how long we last on her pay alone. Maybe two months, if we stop everything. I'd sell the car and get the bus. I'd go to every union meeting and every protest at the gates. And I'd sign up for whatever government help exists the day it exists, no pride about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick. Like I'd want to go back to bed and not get up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Dani's pay would carry you for two months. Does her job feel safer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Safer, yes. She works in a care home, and I can't picture a robot holding Mrs Abara's hand while she cries about her son. But they said that about my job too, didn't they. If they come for hers we've got nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd start doing now, in the next two years, before it arrives?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I keep wanting to say no, I'd just fight it. Maybe I'd get the union to set up a hardship fund now, while people still have wages to put in. That's the only thing I can picture that helps everyone, not just me.

S2.say: This is a choice rich people are making, not the weather. The government has to step in with income support and stop firms from dumping whole shifts overnight.
S2.think: I'm finished at that plant, and the night lead is the first cost they cut. There's nowhere else nearby to go, because the other plant would do the same.
S2.do: Works out with Dani how long they last on Dani's pay alone, about two months, and sells the car. Joins every union meeting and gate protest, pushes for a union hardship fund now, and signs up for government help as soon as it exists.
S2.feel: Sick, like wanting to go back to bed and never get up.
S2.quote: If a robot can fix a stuck ejector pin and swap a mould, then the night lead is the first cost they cut, because nights cost more.
S2.fieldNote: With two years' warning Zoe saw no personal way out, only collective ones: protests, a hardship fund, public support. Thin savings, few local plants and her dislike of retraining leave her with no plan B. She leans on Dani's care home job while admitting she once believed her own job was safe too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. So 2031. I'd be thirty-two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same as before but with a plan behind it. We'd have time to get a law through, a proper one, where companies that replace workers pay into a fund for them. I'd be the annoying woman at every meeting asking what the plan is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is enough time to watch it coming and not enough to become somebody else. I'd see the robots come in press by press. I'd know which month my press goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start saving properly, even if it's sixty a month, and I'd give up the car loan idea and keep the old car going. I'd get onto the union's regional committee so I'm in the room when the deals get made. And I'd make Dani and me talk about days versus nights now, because if I'm losing the job anyway I want the weekends back sooner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Heavy. Less like falling, more like walking into cold water slowly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said five years isn't enough to become somebody else. What would becoming somebody else even look like for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know, and that's the problem. Dani says I'd make a good care worker because I'm bossy and kind. I don't know if I'd go. It feels like giving up on the thing I'm actually good at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you be watching for, in those five years, that tells you it's getting close?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The day they put cameras over the presses that watch the parts. That's what the picker arm on six started with, a camera. When I see cameras on all fourteen, I'll know.

S3.say: We have time to get a proper law through, where companies that replace workers pay into a fund for them. I'd be the one asking what the plan is at every meeting.
S3.think: Five years is enough to watch it coming and not enough to become somebody else. I'd see the robots come press by press and know which month mine goes.
S3.do: Starts saving about 60 a month and drops plans for a newer car. Gets onto the union's regional committee so she's in the room when deals are made, and pushes for a law that makes firms pay into a fund for displaced workers.
S3.feel: Heavy and slow, like walking into cold water.
S3.quote: Five years is enough time to watch it coming and not enough to become somebody else.
S3.fieldNote: The extra three years turned Zoe's panic into dread with a timetable. She'd use the time for politics and a little saving, not for retraining. Dani's suggestion of care work is clearly on the table, but Zoe hears it as giving up her craft.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. 2036. I'd be thirty-seven. That's a long time on the night shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough for a country to get ready if it wants to. Shorter weeks, public jobs, income support. If we don't get those, it's because someone decided we weren't worth it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, with ten years I might actually be fine. Not because the job lasts, it won't, but because I'd have time to get used to the idea. I'm slow with change. Ten years is about my speed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep running nights for a few more years, and I'd fight for a deal where the plant pays for retraining while we're still employed. I'd save what I could. Somewhere around year five I'd probably let Dani talk me into the care course, if it's still a human job by then. Nobody knows that, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but I can breathe. It's like knowing the bill's coming next year, not tomorrow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said with two years you'd sell the car, and with ten you'd wait a few years. What changes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years I'm in a panic and I grab whatever I can. With ten I've got time to be stubborn for a bit and then come round. That's how I've done everything, honestly. Took me two years to agree to move in with Dani.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want the union to win in that decade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Paid retraining while you're still on the payroll, not after you're out. And a rule that the people who built the plant, the operators, get some share of what the robots save. I know that sounds like a dream. Ten years is long enough to dream a bit.

S4.say: Ten years is enough for a country to get ready if it wants to, with shorter weeks, public jobs and income support. If we don't get them, someone decided we weren't worth it.
S4.think: With ten years I might actually be fine, not because the job lasts but because I'd have time to get used to it. I'm slow with change, and ten years is about my speed.
S4.do: Keeps running nights for a few years while the union pushes for paid retraining before layoffs. Saves what she can and expects, around year five, to take a care work course if it's still a human job.
S4.feel: Uneasy but able to breathe, like a bill due next year rather than tomorrow.
S4.quote: I'm slow with change. Ten years is about my speed.
S4.fieldNote: Zoe recognised her own pattern: stubborn first, then she comes round, as she did about moving in with Dani. A decade gives that pattern room to play out, so she can picture a future after the press. She still expects a fight over who shares the savings from automation.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, AGI by 2028. There's no time to be stubborn and then change my mind, and I've got nothing in the bank to buy time with. What would help is money that arrives before the layoff, not after: a fund the company pays into, and income support you don't have to beg for.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who gets the money the robots save. Everyone asks what workers will do. Nobody asks where the savings go. At Kestrel, when the picker arm went on press six, the owners got a new office. Kelly got the supermarket.

headlineQuote: When the picker arm went on press six, the owners got a new office. Kelly got the supermarket.
portrait: Zoe is a 27-year-old night shift lead at a plastics moulding plant, among the best operators on the floor but on lower pay than the plant in the next town, with about three weeks of rent saved. She lives with her partner Dani, a care worker, and never uses AI tools. She sees automation as a fight over who keeps the savings, and her answers move from flat relief in the hype picture to panic when AGI arrives in two years. Her instinct is always the union and the law rather than retraining herself. With ten years' warning she can picture coming round to care work, because she knows she changes slowly.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because there's no time to be stubborn and then adapt, and she has no savings to buy time.
whatWouldHelp: Money that arrives before a layoff rather than after: a fund companies pay into and income support people don't have to beg for.
